title: The One With Phoebes Rats

jokes.text: apparently singing 'I Will Survive' in a helium voice, not helping
jokes.setup: Chandler explains he tried to help Monica decorate for Rachel's birthday party
jokes.punchline: His idea of 'helping' was singing 'I Will Survive' in a helium voice — a comically specific and useless contribution
jokes.explanation: Very Chandler — specific, self-deprecating, and absurd. The specificity of 'helium voice' elevates it beyond a generic 'I tried to help' joke. The deadpan delivery implied by the phrasing 'not helping' lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'll help you decorate!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? That would be great.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I Will Survive! I Will Survive! Hey hey!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: ...What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm helping! In helium voice!

jokes.text: Don't say that loud. Gunther's gonna want to hug me.
jokes.setup: Rachel arrives at the coffee house and someone apparently says her name or greets her warmly
jokes.punchline: Rachel preemptively warns against alerting Gunther, whose unrequited obsession with her is a running gag
jokes.explanation: Relies entirely on audience familiarity with Gunther's running crush on Rachel. Functional running-gag payoff but no new comedic dimension is added. Gets a knowing chuckle from fans.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't speak loudly in here.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Gunther's been staring at me all morning.

jokes.text: Somebody's getting a little fussy. / You're damn right I am. I've been waiting for a cookie for seven minutes.
jokes.setup: Ross says 'Somebody's getting a little fussy,' implying he means baby Emma
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately applies it to himself, complaining he's been waiting for a cookie — the misdirection lands because we expected Ross to be talking about the baby
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirect with excellent economy. The 'seven minutes' detail makes Chandler's petulance specific and funnier. Very much a Chandler joke — adult man acting like a toddler — and the structure is tight. One of the better-constructed jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Somebody's getting fussy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm not fussy. I'm just... I've been waiting for that cookie for twenty minutes.

jokes.text: If I wasn't married, she'd be rejecting me right now.
jokes.setup: Chandler acknowledges Molly the nanny is attractive
jokes.punchline: His self-deprecating spin: even without the marriage obstacle, he'd be struck out — she'd be rejecting him
jokes.explanation: One of Chandler's signature moves: the self-aware, self-deprecating one-liner. The joke is sharp because the punchline undercuts any bravado — he's not saying 'I'd go for her,' he's saying she'd reject him. The word 'right now' makes it perfectly specific. Highly quotable and very Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, she's not that hot. I mean, if she were interested, I'd have no shot anyway. I'd probably say something stupid like, 'Did it hurt?' and she'd be like, 'Did what hurt?' and I'd say, 'When you fell from heaven?' and she'd just stare at me in horror.

jokes.text: Joey's reaction beat — 'How do you think she's doing?' when asked about Molly
jokes.setup: Ross calls out Joey, implying Joey should weigh in on whether Molly is hot
jokes.punchline: Joey plays dumb or deflects by asking 'How do you think she's doing?' — clearly not focused on the same question the others are discussing
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing deflection — either Joey is so distracted by her attractiveness he can't form a real opinion, or he's playing it cagey. Functional character moment but not especially sharp writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's not even that pretty.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, I mean, she's okay, but nothing special.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: [leaves]

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, she is so hot! I'm pathetic!

jokes.text: Am I the only one that doesn't think she's hot? Ross? / I mean, she's not unattractive, but...
jokes.setup: Chandler (married) appeals to Ross to validate that Molly isn't that hot
jokes.punchline: Ross's politically hedged non-answer ('not unattractive, but...') is itself the joke — the cowardly middle ground
jokes.explanation: Ross's wishy-washy hedging is funny but leans on a broad character note. The joke is in the rhythm of the exchange — Chandler fishing for validation and getting nothing useful.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no. The capital of Peru is Vtox.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Phoebe, Lima is the capital of Peru.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, maybe where you're from. In Peru, it's Vtox. It's like detox, but with a V.

jokes.text: Now that Rachel's gone? So hot, I cried myself to sleep last night.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Ross were diplomatically hedging on whether Molly is hot while Rachel was present
jokes.punchline: The moment Rachel leaves, Ross immediately drops all restraint — she's 'so hot I cried myself to sleep'
jokes.explanation: Good escalation payoff — the contrast between Ross's diplomatic 'not unattractive, but...' and his uncensored 'cried myself to sleep' is sharp. Also reveals his desperation in an absurd way. 'Cried myself to sleep' is a funny specific choice.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Is Bob your pet rat?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No! Well, I mean, he is a rat, but he's not a pet. He's more like... a roommate who doesn't pay rent. It's like leaving cookies out for Santa, except the rat actually shows up.

jokes.text: Hey, Mike, what's the capital of Peru? / Lima. / No. / It starts with a V and ends with an X. / And hopefully with a T-O in the middle.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks Mike the capital of Peru and rejects the correct answer ('Lima')
jokes.punchline: She insists it starts with V and ends with X — Mike plays along by suggesting 'Vtox' hopefully containing 'TO' in the middle (Vtox = 'V-TO-x'). Then Phoebe accepts 'Vtox' as the answer.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe absurdism — she's completely wrong but entirely confident. Mike's 'Vtox' gag is a solid payoff. The escalation into Phoebe actually accepting the made-up answer adds a sweet layer of character-consistent logic. The 'hopefully' in Mike's line is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, but Santa doesn't poop in your apartment.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. No, that's Bob. / Well, he's your pet rat? / Well, not so much a pet as, you know, an occasional visitor who I put food out for. Kind of like Santa.
jokes.setup: Mike freaks out seeing a rat; Phoebe casually says it's 'Bob'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe explains Bob isn't a pet — he's more like 'an occasional visitor I put food out for. Kind of like Santa.' The comparison is both logical in Phoebe's worldview and completely absurd.
jokes.explanation: The Santa comparison is genuinely inspired — it follows a weird Phoebe-logic that is both surprising and completely in character. It's the kind of line that makes you laugh AND appreciate the writing. Highly quotable, memorable, and only Phoebe could say it without it seeming forced. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What are leptospirosis and hantavirus?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: They're diseases. And they don't sound very relaxing.

jokes.text: Except Santa doesn't poop on the plate of cookies.
jokes.setup: Phoebe just compared Bob the rat to Santa Claus
jokes.punchline: Mike's dry correction: 'Except Santa doesn't poop on the plate of cookies' — a perfectly logical rebuttal that also happens to be disgusting and funny
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man rebuttal. The logic is immaculate — it's exactly the right way to puncture the Santa analogy. The word 'plate' is specific and gross in the best way. Tight structure: Phoebe sets up absurdity, Mike deflates it with one precise, revolting image. Pairs with joke 9 to form one of the episode's best two-line exchanges.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: You have to get rid of that rat.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But Mike, you eat food that the rat has been near.

jokes.text: I mean, they transmit leptospirosis and hantavirus. / What are those? / I don't know, but they don't sound like spa treatments.
jokes.setup: Mike warns Phoebe about rat-borne diseases — leptospirosis and hantavirus
jokes.punchline: Phoebe doesn't know what they are, and Mike admits he doesn't either but observes they don't 'sound like spa treatments'
jokes.explanation: Mike using scary-sounding disease names he doesn't actually understand is a smart, economical joke. The 'spa treatments' comparison is a clever pivot — using the sounds of words as the comedic vehicle. Tight, well-structured exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. You're apologizing... by insulting me?

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: That's quite an apology technique you've got there.

jokes.text: It's so weird you think he's so gross, yet you're willing to eat his crackers.
jokes.setup: Mike has convinced Phoebe to get rid of Bob the rat
jokes.punchline: Phoebe points out the hypocrisy: Mike finds the rat gross but was apparently eating crackers shared with the rat
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — Mike is disgusted by the rat but unknowingly shared food with it. Phoebe pointing it out with no malice, just genuine confusion, is funny. Slightly predictable but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm so sorry, Gavin. I really want to talk to you about this.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, no problem.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, excuse me! We're trying to have a conversation here!

jokes.text: Is this your first apology?
jokes.setup: Rachel is giving Gavin a lengthy, meandering apology, listing all the bad things she initially thought of him
jokes.punchline: Gavin drily asks if this is her first apology — implying she's doing it badly by recounting all the insults within the apology itself
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — four words that perfectly skewer Rachel's bumbling apology. It's a sharp, witty character observation delivered with Gavin's dry superiority. The joke is structurally ideal: the longer Rachel's setup goes, the more devastating the four-word punchline. Earns a high score for exceptional compression.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: I was looking at your skirt professionally.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: I was focused on your butt and didn't notice anything else.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. Obviously, Heather's ass has something more important to say, so I'll just wait till it's finished.
jokes.setup: Gavin is distracted by a passing woman's rear end while Rachel is mid-apology
jokes.punchline: Rachel sarcastically defers to 'Heather's ass' as if it's a competing speaker, with exaggerated politeness
jokes.explanation: Rachel's indignation is well-channeled into a witty personification of the ass as a conversational partner. The 'I'll just wait till it's finished' adds the right degree of passive-aggressive politeness. Solid workplace comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Are you jealous?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! Please, please, please pay attention to me! Look at me!

jokes.text: Or was it pants? I didn't really see what happened below the ass area.
jokes.setup: Gavin claims he was 'in fashion' and looking at the passing woman's skirt, not checking her out
jokes.punchline: He then admits he doesn't know if it was a skirt or pants because he wasn't looking below the ass area — entirely undermining his own defense
jokes.explanation: Self-defeating alibi humor. Gavin's attempt to explain himself only makes it worse, and the phrase 'below the ass area' is a memorably clinical way to phrase it. Good character work — his obliviousness to his own creepiness is consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it was different because... I don't know, it just was!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And second of all, he's really, really hot.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. I'm jealous. 'Oh, Gavin. Please, please look at my ass.' / Stop looking at my ass!
jokes.setup: Gavin accuses Rachel of being jealous that he was looking at another woman's butt
jokes.punchline: Rachel sarcastically role-plays the jealousy in an exaggerated voice, then immediately snaps 'Stop looking at my ass!' — implying Gavin is now looking at hers during her performance
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke with a great escalation: sarcastic imitation followed by the reveal that in doing so, she's inadvertently directed his attention to her own backside. The snap out of the bit is perfectly timed. Funny and physical even in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: His last name is... I don't know. Wait, who needs a last name? Moses didn't have a last name. Just Moses. Madonna, just Madonna. Cher, just Cher.

jokes.text: That is totally different for two reasons. One: I didn't know that you knew that.
jokes.setup: Gavin calls Rachel a hypocrite for being outraged about his behavior when she slept with her assistant Tag
jokes.punchline: Rachel begins a 'two reasons' rebuttal — but reason #1 is that she didn't know Gavin knew, completely exposing her hypocrisy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-structured jokes. The 'two reasons' format builds anticipation for a logical defense; instead reason #1 is pure panic — 'I didn't know that you knew that' — which is both a confession and a complete dismantling of her moral high ground. The structure is immaculate and the character moment is perfect Rachel. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why do you know so much about Tag?

jokes.text: We had a... We had a deep, meaningful relationship. / What was Tag's last name? / It was... Oh, my God. He didn't... He didn't have a last name.
jokes.setup: Rachel insists her relationship with Tag was meaningful, not superficial like Gavin's ogling
jokes.punchline: Gavin asks Tag's last name; Rachel can't remember it, then tries to rationalize: 'He didn't have a last name. It was just Tag, like Cher or... Moses.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating spiral of Rachel's rationalization — not knowing his last name, then claiming he was mononymous like Cher, then stretching to 'Moses' — is a great comedic descent. The 'Moses' addition is an inspired absurdist touch. Well-paced and funny across multiple beats.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wasn't staring at the nanny!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, you were!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. But in my defense, she does have a great personality.

jokes.text: Tag's last name was Morgan! / It was Jones. / What are you, his boyfriend?
jokes.setup: Rachel triumphantly remembers Tag's last name as 'Morgan'
jokes.punchline: Gavin casually corrects her ('It was Jones'), implying he knows more about her ex than she does, then Rachel deflects with 'What are you, his boyfriend?'
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. Gavin knowing Tag's last name better than Rachel does is a sharp reversal. Rachel's defensive 'What are you, his boyfriend?' is a classic deflection when cornered — well-timed and characteristically Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I prefer a woman where I have to work to find the attractiveness. You know, like, she's got a great personality, and then one day you look at her and you go, 'Wow, I can see how others might find her attractive.'

jokes.text: Man, I wish I had a nanny like you. / You mean when you were a baby? / Sure.
jokes.setup: Joey is flirting with Molly the nanny, openly wishing he 'had a nanny like her'
jokes.punchline: Molly offers him a polite out ('You mean when you were a baby?'); Joey simply says 'Sure' — not correcting the implication, just accepting the charitable interpretation
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. Joey's 'Sure' is the whole joke — he's not correcting Molly, just going with it, which is simultaneously dumb and sly. Only one word delivers the punchline. Very Joey-specific in character and execution.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, that's a great idea. Let's just let Joey win so he feels better about himself.

jokes.text: Would you stop staring at her? / I wasn't staring. I was leering.
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Joey to stop staring at the nanny
jokes.punchline: Joey corrects the verb — not staring, but 'leering' — a distinction that makes it worse, not better
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — the entire joke is in one word: 'leering.' Joey correcting Chandler's characterization by upgrading it to something more inappropriate is a perfect character beat. It's oblivious self-incrimination played as a semantic correction. Very quotable and punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dude, you gotta stop with the baby talk. Emma's gonna think her name is 'Emmie-Wemmie.'

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? It's cute!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's cute when she's two. When she's sixteen and filling out college applications, 'Emmie-Wemmie' is gonna be a problem.

jokes.text: Maybe she's attractive in an obvious kind of way. Yeah, obvious beauty's the worst. You know, when it's right there in your face. Me, I like to have to work to find someone attractive. Makes me feel like I earned it.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Ross, both clearly attracted to the nanny, try to rationalize why they're not bothered by her attractiveness
jokes.punchline: Their increasingly absurd attempts to frame conventional beauty as a negative ('obvious beauty's the worst,' 'I like to work to find someone attractive') expose their transparent denial
jokes.explanation: Decent bit of self-deceptive humor but runs a little long and doesn't have a sharp enough punchline to cap it. The 'earned it' line is the best part — the absurdity of treating physical attraction like a merit badge. Competent but not particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, you're like a child. You want what you can't have.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I am a child!

jokes.text: Looks like Joey's doing all right with her. Yeah. Hey, that was nice of you guys to back off and let Joey get the girl for once.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler observe Joey making moves on Molly
jokes.punchline: Chandler frames it as a generous act of sacrifice — 'letting Joey get the girl for once' — when really they had no actual shot
jokes.explanation: Decent bit of self-deceptive rationalization. The joke is in Chandler reframing their irrelevance as magnanimity. Competent but familiar Friends territory — the 'we're definitely not trying, we're choosing not to' denial.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, Joey, sometimes I look at you and I see Ben. You're both equally mature, you both think with your stomachs, and you both have this inability to think about consequences.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, what are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm just saying you're like a child. And the really uncomfortable part? I'm attracted to you.

jokes.text: They've elected me to talk to you about the baby talk. It's not so good.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been chosen as group spokesperson to deliver feedback to Ross about his baby talk to Emma
jokes.punchline: The formal, diplomatic framing ('they've elected me') for such a trivial and embarrassing message is the joke
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing. The bureaucratic framing for the mundane complaint is in Chandler's wheelhouse. Gets a moderate laugh, nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You need to focus your sexual energy on someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, if you insist.

jokes.text: Bye, Emma! [Ross does baby talk after being told it's embarrassing]
jokes.setup: Chandler has just told Ross that his baby talk is 'not so good' on behalf of the group
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately reverts to baby talk anyway — 'Bye, Emma!' — proving he cannot help himself
jokes.explanation: Solid callback payoff to the baby talk setup. Ross's immediate relapse is funny in its simplicity. Character-consistent and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't care if you like it or not. These appetizers are PERFECT, and if you can't appreciate that, then you can just leave!

jokes.text: So you think I'm just gonna sleep with her and never call her again, and things are gonna get uncomfortable? / Yeah, that sounds about right.
jokes.setup: Ross explains why he doesn't want Joey pursuing Molly the nanny
jokes.punchline: Joey summarizes the concern accurately — 'sleep with her and never call her again' — and Ross confirms that yes, that's exactly it
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-awareness about his own patterns — articulating them clearly — contrasted with Ross's matter-of-fact 'yeah, that sounds about right' is a funny dynamic. The joke is in the lack of offense Joey takes at the accurate characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: No, I'm not killing Bob. I'm just testing his fitness level.

jokes.text: Oh, man! What'd you have to go and say that for? Now that you told me I can't have her, makes me want her even more!
jokes.setup: Ross tells Joey Molly is 'off-limits'
jokes.punchline: Joey's immediate, petulant response — the forbidden fruit effect has instantly intensified his interest, and he's completely unfiltered about it
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey id-driven comedy. The joke is that Joey is completely transparent — there's no internal filter. The 'forbidden fruit' dynamic is a well-worn trope but Joey's honesty about it is specifically funny.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could give it to a nice family. Like, maybe they'll take it to Disneyland and it'll meet Mickey Mouse and they'll become best friends and then maybe Disney will make a movie about it called 'From Rags to Riches: The Mighty Rat' and it'll win an Oscar and I'll cry.

jokes.text: What are you, a child? / Yes!
jokes.setup: Ross rhetorically asks if Joey is a child after his petulant 'forbidden fruit' outburst
jokes.punchline: Joey confirms: 'Yes!' — with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. The joke is entirely in Joey's honest, unashamed affirmation of what Ross intended as a rhetorical put-down. Only two syllables needed. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Her name is still Bob.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: She's a girl. You want to change it?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No! No, Bob is her name. She's always been Bob to me.

jokes.text: Setting rattraps. / To kill Bob? / No. No, to test his neck strength.
jokes.setup: Phoebe sees Mike setting rattraps and asks if it's to kill Bob
jokes.punchline: Mike sarcastically claims it's to 'test his neck strength' — a darkly absurd reframe of what a rattrap obviously does
jokes.explanation: Dark and efficient. 'Test his neck strength' is a sharp, dry euphemism for what a rattrap does to a rat's neck. Nicely subversive for a broad network sitcom. The delivery would be perfectly deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Maybe it was a different rat?

jokes.text: No, I don't want to kill him. I thought we were gonna capture him and set him free in the countryside, where he could meet a friendly possum and a wisecracking owl.
jokes.setup: Phoebe objects to the rattraps and explains her alternative vision
jokes.punchline: The 'countryside' plan escalates from reasonable (capture and release) to a Phoebe-flavored fantasy world involving a 'friendly possum and a wisecracking owl' — as if Bob is a character in a Disney film
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Phoebe — she's genuinely imagined a full animated-movie backstory for Bob. The specificity of 'wisecracking owl' is what elevates this from generic Phoebe-whimsy to a genuinely funny image. Only Phoebe could say this with complete sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm watching Dallas at 2 in the afternoon. What have I become?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, who shot J.R.? Oh man, I've been unemployed so long I forgot how to keep up with current events. Well, current events from 1980.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Bob had babies! Bob's a mom!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been searching for Bob the rat, assuming Bob is male
jokes.punchline: Bob is revealed to have had babies, meaning Bob is female — 'Bob's a mom!'
jokes.explanation: The surprise reveal that Bob is a mother is a good beat. Phoebe's delighted 'Bob's a mom!' reads as genuine excitement rather than crisis, which is funny. The joke then pivots to dark comedy as we realize the trap implication.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What's up? What's up? Could that BE any more outdated? Next you'll be asking me if I want to hang ten or catch some gnarly waves, dude.

jokes.text: We'll have to think of a new name. / I don't know, I kind of like 'Bob' for a girl.
jokes.setup: Mike suggests they need a new name now that Bob is revealed to be female
jokes.punchline: Phoebe defends 'Bob' as a girl's name — a classic Phoebe non-sequitur that sidesteps the actual problem entirely
jokes.explanation: Light Phoebe moment. Her logic is characteristically sideways — the name issue is not the problem, but she's focused on it. Mild and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't trust Joey with the nanny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? I'm a professional actor!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, you showed up to audition for a doctor wearing a stethoscope you bought at a toy store.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was method acting!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You also wore a fake mustache that was clearly drawn on with a marker.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. We killed Bob?
jokes.setup: Mike points out the rattle of a trap; they implied they set a trap; Bob is now gone
jokes.punchline: The realization hits: they killed Bob the rat they were just celebrating as a new mother. The horror-comedy pivot is sharp.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedic beat. The escalation from 'Bob's a mom!' to 'We killed Bob?' in quick succession is an effective tonal swing. The question mark — uncertain, horrified — is the right note.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, any day now. I'm sure companies are just lining up to hire someone who makes jokes during interviews instead of, you know, answering questions.

jokes.text: Well, maybe it wasn't Bob. Maybe it was a mouse. / Susie?
jokes.setup: Mike tries to soften the blow by suggesting the trap caught a mouse, not Bob
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately has a name for the hypothetical mouse — 'Susie?' — revealing she has named every rodent in her apartment
jokes.explanation: Brilliant single-word joke. The implication — that Phoebe has named ALL the rodents and has a whole community of them — is revealed in one syllable. 'Susie?' as a question shows she's not sure if it's Susie, suggesting there might be more. Very high economy score, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is, your entire life goal is to sleep with every woman in New York?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because that's what I'm hearing. You want a good job? Sleep with the boss. You want to be a better actor? Sleep with your acting coach. You want world peace? Sleep with world peace.

jokes.text: Some woman who sounded a lot like Joey called earlier and asked for her daughter, the 'hot nanny.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks Chandler to keep Joey away from Molly; Chandler reveals Joey already called trying to get information about her
jokes.punchline: Joey used a fake woman's voice to call and ask about the 'hot nanny' — the disguise was thin enough that it was 'a woman who sounded a lot like Joey'
jokes.explanation: Good Joey-specific humor — the idea of Joey doing a female voice that's immediately recognizable as Joey is very consistent with his character. Chandler's detached delivery of the report makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, it's very rare to find an attractive nanny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I immediately pictured a tree.

jokes.text: Is this your long-term plan, for me to run interference? Because I could get a job any day now.
jokes.setup: Ross wants Chandler to babysit Joey and prevent him from pursuing Molly
jokes.punchline: Chandler's mock-protest that he has better options — 'I could get a job any day now' — is a self-aware reference to his long unemployment arc, delivered with false dignity
jokes.explanation: Decent reference to Chandler's unemployment arc. The 'any day now' phrasing is delusional optimism that's characteristically Chandler. Gets a solid chuckle from fans who know the arc.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I need to organize my thoughts.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thoughts? Plural?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, my thought.

jokes.text: You do appear right on the cusp of something.
jokes.setup: Chandler semi-seriously claims he could get a job any day now
jokes.punchline: Ross's flat, diplomatic 'You do appear right on the cusp of something' is a perfectly non-committal endorsement that doubles as gentle mockery
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. 'On the cusp of something' is vague enough to be meaningless but sounds like encouragement — perfect passive-aggressive support. Well-compressed and genuinely witty.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's like... she's like a beautiful princess locked away in a tower. And I'm the knight who's gonna rescue her.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The knight who's married.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm a knight having an affair. It's still romantic!

jokes.text: Because you know once Joey sets his mind on something, more often than not, he's going to have sex with it.
jokes.setup: Chandler warns Ross that keeping Joey from Molly may not work for long
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'sets his mind on something... going to have sex with it' treats Joey's libido as an almost mechanical inevitability
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler-narrating-Joey observation. The word 'it' — not 'her,' but 'it' — reduces the target to an object, which is both funny and characterizes Joey's approach efficiently. Solid character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's the most beautiful woman in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you might want to keep that opinion to yourself when Monica gets here.

jokes.text: Nannies like her don't grow on trees. / [Beat] Picturing that tree? / I am, yes.
jokes.setup: Ross says 'nannies like her don't grow on trees' as a figure of speech
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks if Ross is picturing a tree of hot nannies; Ross confirms he is — both men have immediately visualized the absurd literal image
jokes.explanation: Smart and efficient. Taking a cliché literally and making both characters complicit in the absurd image is a clever beat. The rhythm is perfect — the question, the beat, 'I am, yes' — and the visual gag is implied without needing to show anything. Nice meta-awareness of the cliché.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm like a character in a Hemingway novel—strong, silent, mysterious.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, you're like a character in a menu—appetizer.

jokes.text: For a walk. / You mind if I join you? / Actually, I'd rather be alone. You know, I really need to organize my thoughts. / Your thoughts? Plural?
jokes.setup: Joey says he needs to 'organize his thoughts' — implying he has multiple, complex ideas
jokes.punchline: Chandler's mock-shock at 'thoughts? Plural?' — implying Joey's inner life is usually singular at best
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey-is-not-bright joke, done efficiently. Chandler's incredulity at 'plural' is a nicely economical put-down. Not the most original but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Gavin's office.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Hi Mom. No, that's just my secretary.

jokes.text: All right, fine. I only have one thought. / It's about the hot nanny! I gotta see her!
jokes.setup: Chandler questions whether Joey has multiple thoughts; Joey concedes he has only one
jokes.punchline: His single thought is, unsurprisingly, the hot nanny — delivered with desperate urgency
jokes.explanation: Decent callback payoff. Joey's desperation ('I gotta see her!') is funny in its rawness. Expected but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Gavin, I've noticed you staring at women. That's inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes you do. You're always looking at them like... like you're a donkey and they're carrots.

jokes.text: It's like she's the princess and I'm the stable boy.
jokes.setup: Joey is romanticizing his pursuit of the nanny despite the obstacles
jokes.punchline: His framing of a mundane lust as a fairy tale epic — 'princess and stable boy' — is grandiose and self-aggrandizing in a specifically Joey way
jokes.explanation: Joey's romantic mythology-building around a crushingly mundane situation is classic Joey. This setup pays off brilliantly later (see joke 51), so its rewatch value is high.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you know what? You're a jerk!

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Yeah, well I watched you practice that insult for three hours this morning.

jokes.text: Interesting. Now there are obstacles. Hot nanny and me against the world! This is the stuff great novels are made of. / Great novels? / Fine. Mediocre porn.
jokes.setup: Joey learns Ross specifically told Chandler to stop him — increasing the 'forbidden' nature
jokes.punchline: Joey elevates the situation to 'great novels' territory, then immediately self-corrects to 'mediocre porn'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. The arc of 'great novels... mediocre porn' is perfect Joey self-awareness — he reaches for literary grandeur, then honestly corrects himself. The word 'mediocre' is what makes it exceptional: not just 'porn,' but specifically mediocre porn. Only Joey. Highly quotable, great character integration, well-structured escalation-and-deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to take the high road and be the bigger person here.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm not going to say anything mean. I'm just going to say that I hope you find someone who's... well, at your level.

jokes.text: Hello, this is Rachel Greene. How can I help you? / Okay then. I'll pass you back to your son.
jokes.setup: Gavin answers Rachel's phone, claiming she's just 'his secretary'; Rachel grabs it and answers formally as herself
jokes.punchline: Gavin's caller is immediately revealed to be his mother — 'I'll pass you back to your son' — a callback to Rachel earlier calling Gavin a 'mama's boy'
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed callback — the mama's boy accusation pays off immediately and concretely. The 'I'll pass you back to your son' line is delivered with perfect understated satisfaction. Nicely earned.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: I'll come to your party, Rachel. But only because you asked so nicely. After all, you do work for me.

jokes.text: If you like looking at butts so much, why don't you just go look in a mirror?
jokes.setup: Rachel has been building up to a comeback against Gavin for hours (she made a note on a pad)
jokes.punchline: The comeback itself — 'go look in a mirror' — is weak as an insult (calling him a butt), but the meta-reveal that she spent three hours preparing it makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: the insult itself is mediocre (intentionally), and Gavin calling her out for having prepared it for three hours is the real punchline. Meta-structure elevates what would be a weak standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I love your sweater! It's so cute!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, not at all. It's hideous.

dialogue.speaker: Random Person
dialogue.line: Wow, okay then.

jokes.text: Thank God you finally said that. I saw you make a note on your pad three hours ago.
jokes.setup: Rachel delivers her carefully prepared insult about mirrors and butts
jokes.punchline: Gavin reveals he watched her write it down three hours earlier and has been waiting for it — exposing the insult as labored and long-planned
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-comedy. The reveal that Gavin has been patiently waiting for Rachel's laboriously prepared comeback punctures any sense of triumph she had. 'Thank God you finally said that' is a great opener — relief mixed with mockery. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So which do you think - tuna tartare or mushroom empanadas?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, one's raw fish and the other's a fried pocket of sadness, so...

jokes.text: I don't care about you enough to bug me. In fact, from now on, I'm going to take the high road and be very, very nice to you, you mama's boy — starting right now.
jokes.setup: Gavin accuses Rachel of being bugged by him; she claims to not care and announces she'll take the high road
jokes.punchline: She calls him 'you mama's boy' in the same sentence as promising to 'be very, very nice' — unable to maintain the high road for even three words
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-consistent joke. The gap between Rachel's stated intention ('high road, very nice') and her immediate failure ('you mama's boy') is a perfect irony beat. 'Starting right now' after the insult is the precise comedic timing that makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He pushed me because he liked me.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, he pushed you because you were in front of him.

jokes.text: Oh, no, no, no. Gavin can't. He already has plans — most likely with his mother.
jokes.setup: Monica invites Gavin to Rachel's party; Rachel tries to intercept
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'most likely with his mother' — continuing the mama's boy running gag while trying to seem like she's just informing Monica
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag hit. Rachel can't resist the mama's boy dig even when trying to be strategic. Gets a mild laugh on the callback. Not much new added.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, she's very pretty, and she has a great body, and she's always doing these little things that are very—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm a lesbian!

jokes.text: Hey, Mr. Phillips. Nice suit. / Right there. That was so fake!
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Rachel to demonstrate faking niceness; Rachel immediately demonstrates by complimenting a passing Mr. Phillips
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately recognizes it as fake — confirming Rachel's niceness IS always fake
jokes.explanation: Light but effective. The implication that Rachel is always fake in her pleasantries — detectable even to Monica immediately — is a nice character note. Economical setup and payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, shoes! Finally! I've been waiting all day for these!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Before you open that... I need to tell you something.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I may have borrowed your shoebox last week to help some babies.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Babies? Phoebe, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, but they're really cute and they need a home, so...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Baby rats!

jokes.text: Maybe he keeps bothering you so much because he likes you. It's like in first grade when Skippy Lange would push me because he secretly had a crush on me. / Monica, you think Skippy liked you? Honey, all those boys had a bet to see if he could knock you over.
jokes.setup: Monica fondly recalls Skippy Lange pushing her in first grade as a sign he had a crush on her
jokes.punchline: Rachel reveals the truth: the boys had a bet to see if he could knock Monica over — it was bullying, not affection
jokes.explanation: Dark little comedy gem. Monica's warm misinterpretation of childhood bullying as a crush is funny on its own; Rachel's flat correction ('a bet to see if he could knock you over') is devastatingly specific and dark. The 'knock you over' detail implies Monica was a heavy child — a classic Friends meta-reference to Monica's backstory. Well-structured two-beat joke with real bite.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: RATS?! At my party?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God!

jokes.text: Do you see what all the guys see in her? / Wouldn't kick her out of bed. / No more vodka for me.
jokes.setup: Monica, slightly drunk on vodka, is evaluating Molly the nanny
jokes.punchline: Monica accidentally uses a crude male 'wouldn't kick her out of bed' assessment, then immediately self-corrects upon realizing what she said
jokes.explanation: Good drunk Monica moment. The male-gaze idiom coming out of Monica's mouth is funny, and her instant self-awareness — 'no more vodka for me' — is a clean, economical reaction beat. Character-consistent with Monica's control-freak nature catching itself.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not like that as a parent!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh honey, you're not a parent. You're like seventeen parents. Seventeen bad ones.

jokes.text: These are my rat babies! / Yeah. We have rat babies now.
jokes.setup: Phoebe arrives at Rachel's birthday party with a shoebox
jokes.punchline: The shoebox contains the baby rats — Phoebe has brought them to the birthday party, to Rachel's horror
jokes.explanation: Solid physical comedy escalation — bringing rats to a birthday party is a good absurdist payoff. Mike's resigned 'Yeah. We have rat babies now' captures the deadpan despair of being with Phoebe perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You left the party for rats?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: They needed me! And you know what? You're lucky. You have a nanny to help you with Emma. Some of us have to choose between our social life and our responsibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A nanny that you recommended!

jokes.text: So this is what a stroke feels like.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just discovered Phoebe brought rat babies to her birthday party
jokes.punchline: Rachel's reaction isn't anger or disgust — it's a clinical, dissociated observation that she might be having a stroke
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and a genuinely original reaction. Instead of screaming or scolding, Rachel goes somewhere unexpected — calm, clinical, dissociated. 'So this is what a stroke feels like' is both funny and a perfect character beat (Rachel processing an overwhelming situation through self-focused detachment). Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Acting is a discipline, you know? It requires hard work, dedication, studying the craft...

dialogue.speaker: Molly
dialogue.line: Wait, you studied acting?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, no. But I'm saying it requires it.

jokes.text: Are you comparing my daughter to a rat? / No. Seven rats.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Rachel she should understand the responsibility of caring for the rat babies because Rachel is a mother
jokes.punchline: Rachel asks if she's comparing Emma to a rat; Phoebe corrects — not one rat, but seven
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'No. Seven rats.' is structurally perfect — two words that make the joke dramatically worse than the question implied. Phoebe's clarification isn't even a defense; it just escalates the insult. The specificity of seven is key. Very high economy (essentially two words carry the whole punch), perfect character integration (only Phoebe would think this correction helped), and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, yeah, but have you felt this couch? It's not very comfortable.

jokes.text: Hey, where the hell are Joey and Molly? I asked you to watch them. / I'm sorry. I got a little preoccupied. [holds up rat box]
jokes.setup: Ross demands to know where Joey and Molly are, blaming Chandler for failing to watch them
jokes.punchline: Chandler's excuse is that he got 'preoccupied' — with the rat babies, which he's now holding
jokes.explanation: Visual callback gag. The image of Chandler sheepishly holding the rat box as his excuse is funny but not especially sharp writing. Gets the laugh mainly from the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm serious, Ross. I can love two people at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not possible.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes it is! I love you, I love Chandler, I love Phoebe...

jokes.text: So where'd you study? / I didn't go to college. / No, where'd you study acting? / Molly, people don't study acting.
jokes.setup: Joey is explaining to Molly that acting is a serious discipline requiring hard work
jokes.punchline: When Molly asks where he studied, Joey thinks she's asking about college — then when she clarifies she means acting school, Joey dismisses the concept: 'people don't study acting'
jokes.explanation: Smart double-layer joke. Joey first misunderstands 'study' to mean college (revealing his limited frame of reference), then when corrected, dismisses acting education entirely — despite having just claimed acting requires discipline and hard work. The hypocrisy is characteristically Joey and the structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, the nanny has a girlfriend? So she's a lesbian?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh man, that changes everything. Now in my fantasy, it's like... the nanny and her girlfriend are both there, and they're like, 'Joey, we need your help with something,' and I'm like, 'Anything for you ladies.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is even better than I thought.

jokes.text: Will the stable boy never get the princess?
jokes.setup: Joey is about to be cockblocked again when Ross and Chandler intervene
jokes.punchline: Joey dramatically laments in the third person whether he'll 'ever get the princess' — maintaining the fairy tale frame with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A callback to the stable boy metaphor. Joey's commitment to the narrative frame is funny but the joke is running a third iteration at this point and losing some steam.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: They're just doing what comes naturally. When a mommy rat and a daddy rat love each other very much, they... express their feelings in a very special way.

jokes.text: What do you think you were gonna do, have sex with her here on my couch? / No. The leather sticks to my ass.
jokes.setup: Ross bursts in and confronts Joey about pursuing Molly on his couch
jokes.punchline: Joey's denial isn't moral — it's practical: the leather sticks to his ass, so he wouldn't choose this location
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. Joey doesn't deny the intent — only the venue. The leather-sticking-to-his-ass objection is both vulgar and scrupulously logical from Joey's perspective. Only Joey would answer this question this way. Perfect economy, perfect character integration, and the specificity of the leather objection makes it memorable and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! They're doing it! They're doing it right now!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait... that's her mother!

jokes.text: Look, the truth is, I haven't felt this way about anyone since Rachel. I didn't think I could ever love again.
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to convince Ross and Chandler that his feelings for Molly are genuine
jokes.punchline: He invokes his feelings for Rachel — a callback to a previous season storyline — with such sincerity that it undercuts itself; Ross's reaction (he dated Rachel) makes this doubly awkward
jokes.explanation: Works on multiple levels for longtime viewers: Joey genuinely means it, but saying it in front of Ross (Rachel's ex/father of her child) is comically tone-deaf. The earnestness is funny precisely because it's real to Joey. Rewatch value for anyone who followed the season-long arc.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, so if two rats have babies, and then those babies have babies, and then those babies have babies...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: How many rats do you end up with?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because, I mean, I can barely do regular math. Exponential? That's like, a whole other thing.

jokes.text: It's like my favorite fairy tale come true. / Well, Joey, I guess we have no problem. / The princess, the stable boy and the lesbian.
jokes.setup: Molly's girlfriend Tabitha arrives, revealing Molly is a lesbian — instantly defusing the Joey pursuit storyline
jokes.punchline: Joey reframes his 'princess and stable boy' fairy tale (from earlier) to include the lesbian, completing it as 'my favorite fairy tale'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The callback to the 'princess and stable boy' fairy tale setup (joke 43) is perfectly paid off — Joey doesn't react with disappointment or frustration, but with delight, reframing it as his FAVORITE fairy tale. 'The princess, the stable boy and the lesbian' is a genuinely great line: specific, character-perfect, funny on its own, and funnier as a callback. The structure is immaculate. Only Joey could respond this way and make it feel true to the character. Highly quotable, deserves one of the episode's highest scores.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'll give the rats to the lab. But I want a memorial for Bob. Something about how he loved cheese.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A memorial? Phoebe, they're rats.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Not just any rats, Monica. Bob was special. He had refined taste.

jokes.text: When did we become one of those couples whose lives revolve around their rats?
jokes.setup: Mike and Phoebe are preparing formula and changing the rat box — full baby-parent mode
jokes.punchline: Mike pauses to observe that they've somehow become 'one of those couples whose lives revolve around their rats'
jokes.explanation: Funny observational beat. The humor comes from Mike's moment of self-awareness — recognizing they've crossed into absurd 'rat parents' territory — combined with the implied existence of 'those couples.' Riffs on the 'couple who treats pets as children' trope, applied to rats specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I just realized I never told Mike about the triplets!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, I gave birth to my brother's three children and my boyfriend doesn't even know about it.

jokes.text: What happens when they mate and there are hundreds? / Mate? They're all brothers and sisters. / Yeah, not such a problem with rats. They're more of a 'love the one you're with' kind of animal.
jokes.setup: Mike worries about rat population explosion; Phoebe points out they're siblings
jokes.punchline: Mike casually explains that sibling incest 'not such a problem with rats' — framed with the jokey euphemism 'love the one you're with'
jokes.explanation: Nicely dark for a broad network sitcom. The 'love the one you're with' euphemism for rat incest is a clever way to get the joke past the network. Mike's breezy delivery of a genuinely disturbing piece of rodent biology is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'll help you clean up.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, you don't have to do that.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, I want to. It's the least I can do.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, if you insist. Although, honestly, this is kind of my idea of a party.

jokes.text: No. Really? / Oh, my... Get off your sister!
jokes.setup: Mike has explained rat incest; Phoebe is surprised
jokes.punchline: Before either can process it, one of the rats is apparently already doing it — 'Get off your sister!'
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation payoff. The theory immediately becomes practice — Mike has to shout 'Get off your sister!' at a rat seconds after explaining the behavior. The immediacy is what makes it land. 'Get off your sister!' is a great, quotable line. Well-timed and structurally satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Gavin! You finally made it!

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Yeah, sorry I'm late. Traffic was crazy. So where is everyone?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well... they left.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Left? When?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Like three hours ago.

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Three hours? But the party just started!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know! And apparently that's all it took for everyone to decide to leave. So... happy early birthday to me, I guess?

jokes.text: So, what if each of them has seven rats, and then each of those has seven rats? That's like... That's math I can't even do!
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to calculate the rat population explosion
jokes.punchline: She gets partway through the math and gives up — 'That's math I can't even do!' — which is both a character note and an accidental commentary on exponential growth
jokes.explanation: Decent Phoebe moment. 7x7x7 is actually not that hard, which makes her math anxiety funnier. The beat before 'That's math I can't even do!' works with good delivery. Functional character humor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why did you bring a present?

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Well, it's a party. People bring presents to parties. And cake. There's usually cake. And music. You know, basic party stuff.

jokes.text: Well, I know this is gonna sound crazy, but we could not let the box of rats ruin our lives.
jokes.setup: Mike and Phoebe are spiraling about how to manage the rat situation
jokes.punchline: Mike's solution, framed as if it's radical: simply 'not let the box of rats ruin our lives'
jokes.explanation: Nicely dry Mike moment. The framing of a sensible suggestion as if it might be 'crazy' is a good deadpan beat. 'The box of rats ruin our lives' is a funny specific phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Do you have feelings for me?

dialogue.speaker: Gavin
dialogue.line: Yeah, I do. But they're negative feelings.

jokes.text: But to nice families with children and reduced-fat Wheat Thins. / Those were Bob's favorites.
jokes.setup: They agree to give the rats away to nice families
jokes.punchline: Phoebe adds the specific condition: families with 'reduced-fat Wheat Thins,' then Mike confirms those were Bob's favorites — both have deeply humanized the rat's snack preferences
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. The hyper-specific snack condition (reduced-fat Wheat Thins, not regular) is absurdly precise. Mike confirming they were Bob's favorites suggests they've both been feeding the rat branded snacks and tracking its preferences. Nicely weird.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Mr. Whiskers? Mr. Whiskers, baby? Where are you?

dialogue.speaker: Sound Effect
dialogue.line: *squeaking sound*

jokes.text: I guess it just brings back memories, you know, from when I gave birth to my brother's triplets and I had to give them up. / I haven't told you about that yet, have I?
jokes.setup: Phoebe is emotional about giving up the rat babies; she explains why it hits so hard
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually drops the triplet surrogacy story — a major Season 4 storyline — as if Mike might not know yet, then realizes she 'hasn't told him about that yet'
jokes.explanation: Good Phoebe overshare joke. The fact that she treats this enormous biographical revelation as casually as a forgotten errand — and then realizes it might be a first-time disclosure to Mike — is very Phoebe. The 'I haven't told you about that yet, have I?' is a perfect button. Rewatch value for Phoebe fans.

jokes.text: I guess it just brings back memories from when I gave birth to my brother's triplets and I had to give them up.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tearfully says it's hard to let the rats go
jokes.punchline: She explains it's because it reminds her of giving birth to her brother's triplets — an enormous piece of Phoebe backstory dropped casually as an aside
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The delivery depends on context: Phoebe casually name-drops one of the most bizarre facts of her life ('my brother's triplets') as an explanation for being sad about rats. For longtime Friends viewers, this is a known fact about Phoebe, which makes it both a character joke AND a continuity reward. For new viewers, it's completely baffling. 'I haven't told you about that yet, have I?' is the perfect capper — Mike's disorientation mirrors the audience's reaction to the reveal. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: No way. You had your party. Now I have mine.
jokes.setup: Rachel offers to help Monica clean up after the party
jokes.punchline: Monica refuses — she considers cleaning up her party, which she controls entirely by herself
jokes.explanation: Classic Monica control-freak joke. The idea that cleanup is her private pleasure — 'now I have mine' — perfectly encapsulates her character. Gets a solid chuckle from anyone who knows Monica's OCD tendencies.

jokes.text: That jerk, Gavin, from your office didn't show up. / Yeah, I hate him. / [Gavin is standing right there]
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel bond over how happy they are that Gavin didn't show up to the party
jokes.punchline: Gavin has in fact shown up and is standing there, having heard everything
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom cringe setup — talking about someone who's standing behind you. Executed competently but it's one of the most used sitcom conventions. The specific lines ('Yeah, I hate him') are good; the setup is very familiar.

jokes.text: We weren't talking about you. We were... No. No way to recover. No. Okay.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel have been caught badmouthing Gavin to his face
jokes.punchline: Monica starts to deny it, mid-sentence abandons the lie, and declares there's 'no way to recover'
jokes.explanation: Monica's real-time social triage — starting to form a lie, then discarding it and accepting defeat — is a funny, honest beat. The rhythm of 'No. No way to recover. No. Okay.' is well-written. Monica's pragmatic acceptance is very in-character.

jokes.text: Fun party. / Well, it was. And you would have seen it if you didn't show up at... 9:30?! God! This party was lame.
jokes.setup: Gavin makes a remark about the party
jokes.punchline: Rachel's defense of the party falls apart mid-sentence when she hears how late he arrived — 9:30 — and pivots to agreeing 'this party was lame'
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Rachel defends her party and immediately undercuts herself when confronted with evidence that it ended early. Her pivot to 'this party was lame' is funny in its honesty. Classic Rachel.

jokes.text: Again, you're welcome!
jokes.setup: Rachel is not being grateful for the birthday party Monica organized
jokes.punchline: Monica repeats 'Again, you're welcome!' in response to Rachel's self-pity — a sarcastic reminder that she threw the party
jokes.explanation: A running callback to Monica's thanklessness complaint. The 'Again' makes it funnier than a first use — it confirms she's been doing this all episode. Competent but relies on the callback rather than any new construction.

jokes.text: Let me explain how birthday parties usually work. There are presents and a cake, perhaps a fourth or fifth person.
jokes.setup: Rachel questions why Gavin bought her a birthday present
jokes.punchline: Gavin condescendingly explains birthday parties — with the kicker 'perhaps a fourth or fifth person,' implying attendance was tragically low
jokes.explanation: Nicely layered. The condescending tone of 'let me explain how birthday parties work' is funny on its own; the 'fourth or fifth person' detail turns it into a genuine insult about the party's sad attendance. The escalating specificity (presents → cake → 'perhaps' more people) works well.

jokes.text: "From Gavin." / I really mean it.
jokes.setup: Rachel reads the birthday card Gavin wrote; it says simply 'From Gavin'
jokes.punchline: Gavin insists 'I really mean it' — defending his minimal card as heartfelt
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. 'From Gavin' as the entire card message is funny; 'I really mean it' as his sincere defense of two words is perfect deadpan character comedy. Only this specific character — arrogant but somehow earnest — could make this land. Minimal words, maximum payoff.

jokes.text: I do have feelings for you. / You do? / Yes. I feel that you're a little annoying.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Gavin if he has feelings for her (after Monica's theory about why he teases her)
jokes.punchline: Gavin says yes — then reveals the feeling is that she's 'a little annoying' — a bait-and-switch from romantic to dismissive
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The 'I do have feelings for you' setup primes for a romantic confession; the punchline deflects to 'you're a little annoying.' The structure is clean and the deflation is perfectly timed. Highly quotable and sets up the eventual kiss nicely. Character-perfect for Gavin's push-pull dynamic with Rachel.

jokes.text: See, why? Gavin, why? Right when I'm about to change my opinion of you, you go and you... And you do that.
jokes.setup: Rachel was softening toward Gavin after the present, then he delivers his 'you're a little annoying' punchline
jokes.punchline: Rachel's exasperated trailing off — 'you go and you... And you do that' — unable to even articulate what he did
jokes.explanation: Decent reaction beat. Rachel's frustrated vagueness ('you do that') is funny because she's too flustered to name the offense. Functions as a grace note after the stronger joke 74.

jokes.text: No, I think I left one of my rat babies. / Well, no, I haven't seen it, but if I do, I'll let you know. / Rat baby! Rat baby! Rat baby! Rat baby!
jokes.setup: Phoebe returns to Rachel's apartment claiming to have left a rat baby behind
jokes.punchline: Rachel politely says she hasn't seen it — immediately followed by what sounds like a rat baby in the apartment, causing Rachel to frantically call for it
jokes.explanation: Good tag-scene escalation. Rachel's calm 'I'll let you know' immediately followed by a rat baby somewhere in her apartment — leading to both women calling 'Rat baby! Rat baby!' — is a funny ending image. Gets the laugh from the absurdity and the contrast of Rachel's dignified dinner scene and this chaotic coda.

tmdb_overview: Gavin gives Rachel a very interesting birthday gift while Ross begs Joey to stay away from Emma's hot new nanny. Meanwhile, Mike meets and then accidentally murders Phoebe's unusual pet.
insight: Season 9 dips slightly with rat-plot setup jokes landing just under elite threshold at 79.5.
